title: Workers Now Pay $7,471 for Family Cover: Where the Money Goes
summary: KFF's 2026 survey puts the average employer family health premium at $28,303, up 5%, while workers' share jumped 9% to $7,471. On our figures, that $621 increase would absorb about 28% of a 3.7% raise on a $60,000 salary.
description:
Health insurance through work got more expensive again in 2026, and workers carried a bigger share of the rise than their employers. KFF's annual Employer Health Benefits Survey, published on October 22 and based on interviews with 1,937 employers with at least 10 workers, puts the average annual premium for family coverage at $28,303, up 5% from 2025. Single coverage also rose 5%, to $9,804.

The more striking number is what workers pay directly. The average worker contribution for family coverage rose 9%, or $621, to $7,471. For single coverage, workers' share rose $232, or 16%, to $1,672.

This PolicyRix Team analysis breaks down who pays what and what the increase means against pay.

Who pays the premium

On our arithmetic, employers paid about $20,832 of the average family premium, or about 74%, and workers about $7,471, or 26%. For single coverage, employers paid $8,132 and workers $1,672. In monthly terms, a worker with family coverage now pays about $623 a month before any deductibles, copays or coinsurance.

Workers' contributions grew faster than the premium itself because some employers shifted more of the cost onto staff. KFF found 44% of large firms offering benefits increased employees' share of the premium, and 21% raised deductibles or other cost sharing.

Against pay and prices

KFF noted that the 5% rise in family premiums outpaced wage growth of 3.7% and general inflation of 2.7% over the same period. Take an illustrative worker earning $60,000. A 3.7% raise is worth about $2,220 a year before tax. The $621 increase in the average family contribution would take about 28% of that raise. For lower-paid workers, the share is higher, because contributions do not usually scale with salary.

Over five years, KFF says the average family premium has risen 28%.

Small employers are harder hit

The average family premium at small firms, those with 10 to 199 workers, was somewhat lower than at large firms. But small-firm workers often pay far more of it themselves. Nearly one-third of covered workers at small firms were in plans requiring them to pay more than half of the family premium, against 6% at larger firms. For a $27,000 premium, paying half means more than $13,500 a year.

What comes next

The outlook for 2027 is worse. Benefits consultants and insurers point to premium increases approaching double digits next year, driven by hospital prices, specialty drugs including GLP-1 weight-loss medicines, and higher use of care. KFF found 18% of employers raised workers' share of premiums in 2026 in anticipation.

What workers can do

During open enrollment, compare the total cost of each plan, not just the paycheck deduction: add the annual premium contribution to the deductible and the out-of-pocket maximum to see the worst case. If a high-deductible plan comes with a health savings account and employer contribution, it can be cheaper overall for healthy households. Check whether covering a spouse who has access to their own employer plan costs extra; many employers add a spousal surcharge. Use flexible spending or health savings accounts to pay predictable costs with pre-tax money.

What the data cannot tell us

The survey reports averages across firms; individual plans vary widely by region, industry and plan type. Contribution figures exclude deductibles and other out-of-pocket costs, which have also risen. The wage comparison uses national averages, and our salary example is illustrative. And the survey covers employers with 10 or more workers, so it does not describe the smallest businesses or people buying coverage on their own.

The short version: employer health premiums rose faster than pay again, and workers absorbed a growing share of the increase, with bigger rises likely in 2027.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of the KFF 2026 Employer Health Benefits Survey, with reporting from Fierce Healthcare, Healthcare Finance News and Becker's
image_alt: Doctor using a tablet in a clinic (illustrative)
key_points: Average family premium: $28,303, up 5%; single: $9,804, up 5%.
Workers' family contribution rose 9% ($621) to $7,471; single contribution rose 16% to $1,672.
Employers pay about 74% of the family premium on our calculation; workers about $623 a month.
The $621 rise would absorb about 28% of a 3.7% raise on a $60,000 salary.
Nearly one-third of small-firm workers pay more than half of the family premium, against 6% at large firms.
why_it_matters: About half of Americans get health coverage through work. When contributions rise faster than pay, the increase eats into raises and makes job and plan choices more important.

title: Annuity Sales Hit $126bn as Buyers Shift From Fixed to Market-Linked
summary: US annuity sales reached a record $126.3 billion in the third quarter, the 12th straight quarter above $100 billion. Market-linked RILAs jumped 22% while fixed indexed annuities fell 8%. We break down the mix and what it means for buyers.
description:
Americans are buying annuities at a record pace. LIMRA reported US annuity sales of $126.3 billion in the third quarter of 2026, up 4% from a year earlier and the 12th consecutive quarter above $100 billion. Sales in the first nine months reached $355 billion, up 2%.

Underneath the record, the mix is changing. Products tied to stock market performance are growing quickly, while some fixed products are shrinking. This PolicyRix Team analysis breaks down where the money went and what buyers should watch.

The mix in the third quarter

Using LIMRA's figures, our breakdown of third-quarter sales is:

Fixed-rate deferred annuities: $44.5 billion, about 35% of sales, up 2%.
Fixed indexed annuities (FIAs): $30.7 billion, about 24%, down 8%.
Registered index-linked annuities (RILAs): $25.3 billion, a record and about 20%, up 22%.
Traditional variable annuities: $18.2 billion, about 14%, up 11%.
Single premium immediate annuities (SPIAs): $4.1 billion, about 3%, up 6%.
Deferred income annuities: $1.3 billion, about 1%, down 1%.

Through September, RILA sales reached $69.7 billion, up 21%, already about 88% of the record $79.6 billion sold in all of 2025. Fixed-rate deferred sales were down 6% for the year to date and FIAs also down 6%.

Why buyers are shifting

Fixed-rate deferred annuities work like a CD from an insurer: a guaranteed rate for a set number of years. They sold heavily when interest rates jumped in 2023 and 2024. Many of those contracts are now reaching the end of their guarantee periods, and the money is being reinvested, sometimes into new fixed contracts and sometimes into products with more growth potential.

RILAs offer a share of stock index gains up to a cap, in exchange for limits on losses: a buffer absorbs the first slice of a fall, or a floor caps the maximum loss. LIMRA's Keith Golembiewski said investors value that combination of upside and protection. Strong stock markets have also lifted traditional variable annuities, which invest directly in funds.

A caveat on the record

From January 2026, LIMRA's definition of sales includes money paid into new and existing contracts, including certain internal transfers and exchanges. That means reported sales now cover more than new purchases, so comparisons with earlier years overstate growth somewhat.

What buyers should check

Annuities can provide guaranteed income or protected growth, but they are long-term contracts with costs. Before buying, check the surrender period, which can last seven to ten years with charges for early withdrawals; the cap, participation rate and buffer or floor on any index-linked product, and whether the insurer can change them at renewal; annual fees, especially on variable annuities and riders; and the insurer's financial strength rating, since guarantees depend on the insurer. Compare a fixed annuity's rate with CDs and Treasury bonds of the same term after tax. And be wary of advice to swap one annuity for another: an exchange can restart surrender charges and may benefit the seller more than the buyer.

What the data cannot tell us

Sales figures show money flowing in, not whether buyers chose well or what they paid in fees. The 2026 definition change makes year-on-year comparisons imperfect. The data does not show how much is replacement of maturing contracts versus new savings. And product shares can shift quickly if interest rates or stock markets move sharply.

The short version: annuity demand remains at record levels, but the money is moving from fixed guarantees toward market-linked products, which come with more moving parts for buyers to understand.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of LIMRA's US Individual Annuity Sales Survey (Q3 2026), via InsuranceNewsNet and ThinkAdvisor
image_alt: Calculator and financial documents on a desk (illustrative)
key_points: US annuity sales hit a record $126.3 billion in Q3 2026, up 4%, the 12th straight quarter above $100 billion.
RILAs rose 22% to a record $25.3 billion; fixed indexed annuities fell 8% to $30.7 billion.
Fixed-rate deferred annuities remain the biggest category at about 35% of sales on our calculation.
Nine-month RILA sales of $69.7 billion are already about 88% of 2025's full-year record.
LIMRA's 2026 definition now includes some transfers and exchanges, which flatters growth comparisons.
why_it_matters: Annuities are a major retirement savings product. Knowing where buyers are moving, and why, helps savers ask the right questions about caps, fees and surrender charges.

title: Medicare 2027 Is Final: Part B at $209.40, Deductible $292
summary: CMS has finalised 2027 Medicare costs: the standard Part B premium rises $6.50 to $209.40 and the deductible $9 to $292. On our example, a $2,000 monthly Social Security benefit keeps about $65.50 of its $72 cost-of-living raise after the Part B increase.
description:
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services announced the final 2027 Medicare premiums and deductibles on November 17. The standard monthly Part B premium will be $209.40, up $6.50 from $202.90 in 2026. The annual Part B deductible rises $9, to $292. The final premium came in $0.10 below the $209.50 projected in this year's Medicare Trustees Report, which our November 14 explainer used while the figure was pending.

CMS said the increases reflect projected growth in health care spending. This PolicyRix Team analysis sets out the full changes and what they mean for a typical beneficiary.

What changes in 2027

Part B standard premium: $209.40 a month, up 3.2%.
Part B deductible: $292 a year, up 3.2%.
Part A inpatient hospital deductible: $1,776 per benefit period, up $40, or about 2.3%.
Part A premium for people who must buy it: $597 a month, up $32. Most people pay no Part A premium because they or a spouse paid Medicare taxes for at least 10 years.

Higher-income beneficiaries pay more for Part B and Part D through income-related monthly adjustment amounts, which are based on tax returns from two years earlier.

The annual cost

On our arithmetic, a beneficiary paying the standard premium and meeting the full deductible will pay $2,804.80 for Part B in 2027: 12 premiums of $209.40 plus $292. In 2026 the same total was $2,717.80. The increase is $87 a year, before the 20% coinsurance that Part B charges on most services after the deductible.

How much of the COLA is left

Social Security benefits rise 3.6% in January under the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment announced in October. For most retirees, the Part B premium is deducted from their Social Security payment.

Take an illustrative retiree with a $2,000 monthly benefit. A 3.6% COLA adds $72 a month. After the $6.50 Part B increase, the net rise in their payment is about $65.50, so the Part B change takes about 9% of the COLA. For someone with a $1,200 benefit, the COLA adds $43.20, and Part B takes about 15% of it. Lower benefits lose a larger share. A hold-harmless rule prevents the Part B increase from reducing a person's net Social Security payment below the previous year for most beneficiaries whose premiums are deducted from their benefits.

What still varies

Part B is only one piece. Medicare Advantage and Part D drug plan premiums vary by plan and area, and some plans are changing benefits or networks for 2027. Our November 14 explainer covers the Part D out-of-pocket cap, which rises to $2,400 in 2027. Medigap premiums are set by private insurers and also change each year.

What to do before December 7

Medicare open enrollment ends on December 7. Use the Medicare Plan Finder to compare total yearly costs, including premiums, deductibles and expected drug costs, for your own prescriptions. Check whether your doctors and pharmacies remain in network for any Medicare Advantage plan. If your income has dropped since 2024, for example after retirement, you can ask Social Security to recalculate any income-related surcharge using Form SSA-44. And people with limited income should check eligibility for Medicare Savings Programs, which can pay the Part B premium.

What the data cannot tell us

Our COLA examples use round illustrative benefits; actual payments depend on each person's benefit and deductions. The annual Part B total assumes the full deductible is met and excludes coinsurance. Plan-level costs for Medicare Advantage and Part D depend on where people live and what they take, so the standard figures are a floor, not a full budget.

The short version: Medicare's 2027 increases are modest, about $87 a year for the standard premium and deductible, and most retirees will keep the bulk of their cost-of-living raise.
source_name: CMS 2027 Medicare Parts A and B premiums and deductibles fact sheet (November 17, 2026), Federal Register notice, AHA, MOAA and Kiplinger
image_alt: Older couple reviewing paperwork at a kitchen table (illustrative)
key_points: The 2027 standard Part B premium is $209.40, up $6.50; the deductible is $292, up $9.
The Part A hospital deductible rises $40 to $1,776; the Part A premium for those who buy it rises $32 to $597.
Standard Part B premium plus full deductible totals $2,804.80 in 2027, up $87 on our calculation.
On a $2,000 monthly benefit, the 3.6% COLA adds $72 and about $65.50 remains after the Part B rise.
Open enrollment for Medicare Advantage and Part D ends December 7.
why_it_matters: About 68 million people rely on Medicare. The final numbers let retirees budget for 2027 and compare plans before open enrollment closes.

title: UK Car Insurance: Official Prices Up 8%, but Drivers Paid 2% More
summary: The ONS says UK car insurance prices rose 8% in the year to October, the fastest since mid-2024, while the ABI says the average premium paid was only 2% higher at GBP 562. We explain the gap and what EY's forecast of 12% rises in 2027 could mean.
description:
Two official-looking numbers on UK car insurance are telling different stories. Consumer price data from the Office for National Statistics shows motor insurance prices up 8% in the year to October 2026, from 6% in September and the steepest annual rise since June 2024. Yet the Association of British Insurers says the average premium customers actually paid in the third quarter was GBP 562, only about 2% higher than a year earlier.

This PolicyRix Team analysis explains why the two differ, and which one a driver should pay attention to.

The numbers side by side

ONS motor insurance index: up 8% year on year in October, and up 1.3% in the month alone. It turned positive in December 2025 after a long slide that bottomed at minus 13.4% in March 2025.
ABI average premium paid: GBP 562 in the third quarter, about 2% higher than a year earlier.
Defaqto's measure of the most competitive quoted motor premiums: 2.7% higher at the end of September, the first annual rise since 2023.

On our arithmetic, the gap between the ONS and ABI measures is about 6 percentage points.

Why they differ

The ONS tracks the price of broadly comparable cover over time, closer to what a customer would see if they renewed the same policy without changing anything. The ABI averages what customers actually paid across many policies. That average is pulled down when drivers switch to cheaper insurers, choose higher excesses, drop optional extras or buy cheaper cover. In a rising market, the ABI figure tends to lag because people work harder to keep their bill down.

So a driver who renews without shopping around is more likely to see an increase close to the ONS figure. A driver who compares quotes and adjusts cover may see something closer to the ABI figure, or even a fall.

Why prices are rising

Claims are expensive. The ABI says insurers paid a record GBP 3.2 billion in motor claims in the third quarter, up 8% year on year, with the average claim steady at about GBP 4,900. Vehicle maintenance and repair prices rose 5.2% in the year to October in the ONS data. Consultancy EY expects motor insurers to pay about GBP 1.08 in claims and costs for every GBP 1 of premium in 2026, meaning an underwriting loss.

EY has pencilled in premium rises of 4% in 2026 and 12% in 2027. Applied to the ABI's GBP 562 average, our illustration suggests about GBP 584 after a 4% rise and about GBP 655 if a further 12% followed, an increase of about GBP 93 over two years. These are not forecasts for any individual driver.

Home contents is turning too

The ONS contents insurance index was still 5.3% lower than a year earlier in October, but that was the smallest fall since May 2025, and prices rose 1.2% in the month, the biggest monthly rise since May 2024. The overall ONS insurance index, covering motor, home, health and other cover, rose 4.7% to its highest level since the series began in 1988.

What drivers can do

Compare quotes three to four weeks before renewal, when prices tend to be lower than on the renewal date. Check that like-for-like cover is being compared, including the excess and courtesy car. UK pricing rules mean an insurer cannot charge a renewing customer more than a new customer with the same profile through the same channel, but other insurers may still be cheaper. Paying annually avoids interest on monthly instalments. Young drivers can look at telematics policies.

What the data cannot tell us

The ONS index measures price changes for representative policies, not individual quotes. The ABI average mixes many types of cover and drivers. Neither shows regional differences, which are large. And forecasts depend on claims costs, which can change quickly.

The short version: car insurance prices are rising again, faster than the average bill suggests, and drivers who shop around will feel the least of it.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of ONS consumer price data (October 2026), ABI motor premium tracker (Q3 2026), Defaqto and EY, via Insurance Business and Insurance Times
key_points: ONS motor insurance prices rose 8% in the year to October, the fastest since June 2024.
The ABI average premium paid was GBP 562 in Q3, only about 2% higher, a gap of about 6 points.
The ONS tracks comparable cover; the ABI average reflects switching, higher excesses and cheaper cover.
Motor claims hit a record GBP 3.2 billion in Q3; EY expects premiums to rise 4% in 2026 and 12% in 2027.
The ONS overall insurance index reached its highest level since the series began in 1988.
why_it_matters: Most UK drivers renew every year. Understanding why headline figures differ helps them see that shopping around is the main way to avoid the full rise.

title: Ontario Approves Car Insurance Rate Cuts, but Quotes Are Still Rising
summary: Ontario's regulator approved average rate cuts of 0.23% to 5.30% for nine insurer filings taking effect from August to November 28, yet quote data shows premiums up 4.45% to an average of C$2,132. We explain why both can be true.
description:
Ontario drivers are getting mixed signals about car insurance. The Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA) has approved average rate decreases for nine insurer filings, taking effect on renewals between August and November 2026. Yet comparison site MyChoice found average Ontario premiums up 4.45% year on year in 2026, to about C$2,132, based on quotes from January to June.

This PolicyRix Team analysis sets out the approved changes, explains why they can coexist with rising quotes, and what drivers should do at renewal.

The approved changes

According to FSRA's rate approval database, as compiled in August, approved average changes include:

The Personal (Desjardins): minus 5.30%, from November 28.
Heartland Farm Mutual: minus 4.62%, from August 15.
Certas Direct and Certas Home and Auto (Desjardins): minus 2.00% each, from November 28.
Aviva General: minus 1.64%, from September 1.
Allstate: minus 1.64%, from September 15.
Pembridge (Allstate): minus 1.45%, from September 15.
Definity: minus 1.31%, from September 1.
Wawanesa: minus 0.23%, from September 1.
S&Y Insurance (Aviva) was approved for an increase of 1.19%.

These are averages across each insurer's Ontario customers. An individual driver's premium can rise even when their insurer's average falls, depending on claims, driving record, vehicle and postal code.

Why quotes still rose

The MyChoice figures cover quotes from the first half of 2026, before most of the approved cuts took effect and before the July 1 reform that made many accident benefits optional. So the two measures cover different periods. The cuts are also small: on our arithmetic, a 2% cut on the C$2,132 average is about C$43 a year, and even the largest approved cut, 5.3%, is about C$113. Against that, a 4.45% rise implies the average was about C$2,041 a year earlier, an increase of about C$91.

Costs remain high. MyChoice points to repair costs for cars with advanced sensors and cameras, accident rates, fraud and auto theft losses that, while falling in most GTA areas, remain well above pre-pandemic levels.

Where you live matters most

Location is still the biggest factor. MyChoice puts Brampton's average at C$3,471 and Scarborough's at C$3,047, against C$1,680 in Ottawa. On our calculation, Brampton drivers pay about 2.1 times what Ottawa drivers pay. The steepest rises were in Vaughan, up 8.86%, Kingston and Milton.

The July reform

Since July 1, Ontario drivers can opt out of several accident benefits, including income replacement, caregiver, non-earner, housekeeping, death and funeral benefits, while medical, rehabilitation and attendant care remain mandatory. Our October analysis found opting out saves roughly C$100 a year for many drivers but can leave serious gaps for people without workplace disability or life insurance.

What drivers can do

At renewal, ask whether your insurer's approved rate change applied to you and why your premium moved. Compare quotes from several insurers or a broker, since cuts are not automatic and other insurers may price your profile differently. Review the optional accident benefits carefully against your existing disability and life cover before dropping them. Consider a higher deductible if you could afford it, an anti-theft device, winter tires or a telematics programme for discounts.

What the data cannot tell us

The approved changes are as recorded in mid-August and more may have been approved since. Quote averages depend on the drivers who used one comparison site and are not the same as premiums paid. And averages hide big differences between drivers in the same city.

The short version: some Ontario insurers are trimming rates, but the cuts are small and premiums are still drifting up in many cities, so comparing quotes matters more than the headlines.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of FSRA rate approvals (as compiled by Money.ca and Immigration News Canada) and MyChoice's 2026 Ontario Car Insurance Market Overview
key_points: FSRA approved average cuts of 0.23% to 5.30% for nine insurer filings, effective August to November 28.
The Personal (Desjardins) has the largest cut at 5.30%; S&Y Insurance was approved for a 1.19% rise.
MyChoice quote data shows Ontario premiums up 4.45% in 2026 to about C$2,132.
A 2% cut on that average is about C$43; the largest cut is worth about C$113 on our calculation.
Brampton drivers pay about 2.1 times Ottawa drivers, at C$3,471 versus C$1,680.
why_it_matters: Ontario has some of Canada's highest car insurance costs. Knowing that approved cuts are averages, and small ones, helps drivers push for a better price at renewal.

title: Coface Profit Falls 12% as Large Trade Credit Claims Return
summary: French trade credit insurer Coface reported nine-month net income of EUR 155.5 million, down 11.8%, as the cost of claims rose 10.8% with the return of large losses. It is cutting credit limits on riskier buyers while corporate defaults stay at record levels.
description:
Coface, one of the world's largest trade credit insurers, says business failures are still running at record levels and large claims are back. The Paris-based company reported net income of EUR 155.5 million for the first nine months of 2026, down 11.8% from EUR 176.3 million a year earlier, including EUR 47.7 million in the third quarter.

What changed

The number of claims was almost unchanged, down 0.9%, but the amount provisioned for them rose 10.8% because large claims returned in the third quarter. On our arithmetic, that implies the average provision per claim rose by roughly 12%. Chief executive Xavier Durand said corporate defaults remained at a record high, producing larger claims for credit insurers.

The loss ratio after reinsurance still improved, by 1.9 points to 37.7%, helped by releases from reserves set aside in earlier years. Coface responded to the higher risk by stepping up what it calls prevention measures: reviewing and cutting the credit limits it grants on riskier buyers. For brokers and clients, that means more buyer limits under review, particularly in sectors where failures are concentrated.

Revenue rose 1.7% at constant exchange rates and scope to EUR 1,413.3 million. Insurance revenue grew only 0.6% to EUR 1,136 million in a competitive market, while services such as business information and debt collection grew 7.6% to EUR 277.7 million. Investment income rose 47.5% to EUR 67 million, but insurance finance expenses jumped from EUR 0.9 million to EUR 39.5 million, including an EUR 11.7 million foreign exchange loss, which absorbed the gain. Annualised return on average tangible equity fell 0.7 points to 10.7%.

Why it matters for businesses

Trade credit insurance protects companies when customers fail to pay for goods and services bought on credit. It is widely used by exporters and suppliers in Europe and increasingly elsewhere. When insurers cut the credit limit on a buyer, the supplier either has to reduce sales on credit to that customer, ask for payment up front, or carry the risk itself. Limit cuts can therefore spread financial stress through supply chains, as happened during the 2008 financial crisis.

Our earlier analysis of the credit insurance market found it protected a record EUR 9.58 trillion of trade in 2025, but that its share of world trade had slipped to 14% as insolvencies rose for a fifth straight year. Coface's results suggest those pressures are continuing into 2026.

What policyholders should do

Businesses with trade credit cover should expect closer scrutiny of buyers in weaker sectors and countries. Keep insurers informed early about any payment delays, since late notice can affect claims. Review your largest customer exposures and have a plan if a limit is reduced, such as shorter payment terms or letters of credit. When renewing, compare insurers on limit stability and claims service, not just price, and ask a broker how each insurer handled limit cuts in past downturns.

The bigger picture

Credit insurance prices have been falling because of competition, even as claims rise, which squeezes insurers' margins. Coface has been building non-insurance revenue to offset that. Its solvency remained strong at the end of 2025, at about 197%, above its 155% to 175% target range, giving it room to absorb losses. For suppliers, that means insurers are likely to keep a close eye on buyer limits through the winter. The fourth quarter, which often brings year-end insolvencies, will show whether the return of large claims is a blip or a trend.
source_name: Coface Q3 2026 results release, Insurance Business, Reinsurance News and Idéal Investisseur
key_points: Coface's nine-month net income fell 11.8% to EUR 155.5 million; Q3 was EUR 47.7 million.
Claim numbers fell 0.9% but provisions rose 10.8% as large claims returned.
The loss ratio still improved 1.9 points to 37.7%, helped by reserve releases.
Coface is cutting credit limits on riskier buyers as corporate defaults stay at record highs.
Insurance finance expenses rose to EUR 39.5 million, offsetting a 47.5% rise in investment income.
why_it_matters: Credit insurers decide how much trade credit suppliers can safely extend. When they cut limits, businesses must tighten payment terms, which can ripple through supply chains.
